h1:
Khao Ito Waterfall
+ Chakkraphong Reservoir, a Breezy Foothill Escape
intro: Khao Ito is the foothill near town where Prachinburi locals drive out to beat the heat without taking a day off work. It's barely a dozen kilometres from downtown, yet you get a low tiered waterfall shallow enough to soak your feet in, the wide Chakkraphong Reservoir that catches a cool breeze all day, and a quiet, shady cycling loop around the hill. Half a day is enough to see it all, and if you want to stay over you can pitch a tent right by the water.

blocks.html: When people think of Prachinburi, a lot of them picture this side of Khao Yai, or the Chao Phraya Abhaibhubejhr Hospital. But ask people in town where they go on a slow morning off and one answer comes up again and again: Khao Ito. It's close — under half an hour's drive gets you to the foothills — and the air turns shady and cool the moment you arrive.

There are three things to do in the same area: Khao Ito Waterfall, where the stream runs over rocks in low steps; Chakkraphong Reservoir, a wide lake that catches the breeze; and the cycling loop around the hill that Prachinburi riders love to train on. Here's how each spot actually is, how to get there, and when to go to make it worth the trip.

blocks.text: Khao Ito Waterfall — a low stream to soak your feet, not a towering cascade

blocks.html: Let's be straight up front so you're not disappointed — Khao Ito Waterfall isn't a tall curtain of water you stand and pose in front of. It's a stream that tumbles over rocks in low steps, with small pools alternating with flat rock you can sit on and dip your feet in. The water isn't deep and doesn't run hard, so kids can play in it and adults can dangle their legs and cool off easily.

The waterfall sits inside Khao Ito Waterfall Forest Park, an "urban forest" area managed by the Royal Forest Department. Its source comes from the Khao Ito range, so there's usually some water to see nearly year round. But the time it looks best and runs nicely cool is the rainy season into early winter, roughly July to January. In the dry season the water thins out to barely a trickle.

items: Open around 8:00 AM–4:30 PM daily — it's a forest park, not a national park, so the entry fee is modest and at times barely charged. Bring some cash for a small maintenance or parking fee just in case.
The rock is slippery — wear closed-heel shoes or rubber water shoes for the stream, and don't go onto the rocks in flip-flops.
There aren't many shops at the waterfall itself — bring your own drinking water and snacks, and pack your rubbish back out. This area relies entirely on visitors cooperating.

blocks.title: Going early pays off
blocks.html: Mid-morning before noon there are still few people, the rock is open, and the sun isn't harsh yet — perfect for a long soak. Come on a long-weekend afternoon and it starts filling up, and the parking near the waterfall goes fast.

blocks.text: Chakkraphong Reservoir — a wide lake, a cool breeze, mountains all around

blocks.html: Not far from the waterfall is Chakkraphong Reservoir (some locals just call it Khao Ito Reservoir), a royal-initiative reservoir built to store water for local farmers to use in the dry season. But from a visitor's point of view, it's a wide lake ringed by mountains with a cool breeze almost all day.

The spot people like to stand at is the dam crest and the viewing deck, looking out over water that reflects the light against a backdrop of hills. From some angles you can see a large Buddha image up on the hill too. Just pulling up, opening the car doors to the breeze, and sitting with a coffee is already worth the petrol.

items.name: Dam crest + viewing deck
items.blurb: Stroll the dam crest in the breeze, with a viewpoint to photograph the lake against the hills. The light is best in the late afternoon.

items.name: Lakeside camping ground
items.blurb: A wide grass field by the lake where you can pitch a tent overnight. Quiet, clear skies, plenty of stars — bring your own gear.

items.name: Large Naga-sheltered Buddha image
items.blurb: A large Buddha image sheltered by the Naga on the hillside. Stop in to pay respects and take photos along the way.

blocks.title: Bring your own camping gear
blocks.html: The camping ground here is about the natural setting, not a full-service campsite. Facilities are limited, so bring your own tent, water, torch, and food, and pack all your rubbish back out.

blocks.text: The cycling loop around the hill — why Prachinburi riders love it here

blocks.html: A good thing many people don't know about is that Khao Ito has a cycling loop around the hill that's quiet, shady, and keeps changing scenery. Prachinburi riders often drive in with their bikes, drop them, and ride the full loop past bamboo groves, rice fields, the waterfall, the reservoir, and the temple stops.

items: The full loop is about 25 km — passing rural life, bamboo groves, Khao Ito Waterfall, Chakkraphong Reservoir, the Magnetic Hill, and temple stops along the way.
Best for riders with some base fitness — there are short climbs to work for, but nothing brutal; beginners taking it slow can manage.
There's a Magnetic Hill along the way — an optical illusion where a car seems to roll uphill on its own, a fun photo stop.
Set off early — the air is cooler and there's less traffic, so it's safer than later in the morning when the sun starts to bite.

blocks.html: If you didn't bring a bike, you can still have a great time by car — drive the same loop, stopping at each point: the waterfall, the reservoir, and the temple. Half a day is plenty.

blocks.text: A half-day Khao Ito trip — starting from downtown Prachinburi

items.activity: Leave downtown Prachinburi, drive along Suwannason Road into Ban Phra subdistrict
Arrive at Khao Ito Waterfall, walk the rock terrace, soak your feet in the shallow stream
items.note: Going early means fewer people and the sun isn't harsh yet

items.activity: Drive on to Chakkraphong Reservoir, walk the dam crest in the breeze, photograph the lake against the hills
items.note: Park up, open the doors to the breeze, enjoy the coffee you packed

items.activity: Stop at the large Naga-sheltered Buddha image on the hillside to pay respects and take photos
items.note: It's on the same route, no detour needed

items.activity: Head back into town for boat noodles or local Prachinburi food for lunch
items.note: Follow up with a cafe or the Abhaibhubejhr herb garden in the afternoon

blocks.title: If you want to stay over
blocks.html: If you're not rushing back, you can camp by the reservoir, then wake up to a cool morning breeze and thin mist over the water — an atmosphere you won't find in town.

blocks.text: How to get there, where to park, what to bring

items: Location: Ban Phra subdistrict, Mueang Prachinburi district, inside Khao Ito Waterfall Forest Park, with Suwannason Road as the main route.
From downtown Prachinburi: about 10–15 km, a 20–25 min drive — the entrance is fairly clear and signposted.
Public transport is scarce: coming by car or motorbike is by far the easiest; there's no convenient bus access.
Bring cash for a possible maintenance or parking fee, plus drinking water, water shoes, and a rubbish bag.
Best time: rainy season into early winter (Jul–Jan) for more water and cooler air — in the dry season the waterfall dries up a lot.

faq.q: Is Khao Ito Waterfall pretty? Does it have a lot of water?
faq.a: It's a low tiered waterfall running over rocks, not a tall cascade, so it's better for soaking your feet and relaxing than for photographing a curtain of water. There's plenty of water and it runs cool from the rainy season into early winter (July–January); in the dry season the water drops a lot.

faq.q: Are Chakkraphong Reservoir and Khao Ito Waterfall in the same place?
faq.a: They're in the same area — Khao Ito Waterfall Forest Park in Ban Phra subdistrict, Mueang Prachinburi district. Driving from the waterfall to the reservoir takes just a few minutes, so you can do both back to back in one trip easily.

faq.q: Can you camp at Khao Ito? How much does it cost?
faq.a: Yes, you can camp by Chakkraphong Reservoir on a wide grass field by the water — quiet, but with limited facilities, so bring your own tent, water, and food. The cost is modest and at times barely charged; bring some cash for a maintenance fee just in case.

faq.q: Is Khao Ito far from downtown Prachinburi?
faq.a: Very close — about 10–15 km from town, a 20–25 min drive along Suwannason Road into Ban Phra subdistrict. Coming by car or motorbike is easiest, since public transport access is limited.

faq.q: Does Khao Ito really have a cycling route?
faq.a: Yes — it's a loop around the hill of about 25 km, passing bamboo groves, rice fields, the waterfall, Chakkraphong Reservoir, the Magnetic Hill, and temple stops. It suits riders with some base fitness; set off early for cooler air and less traffic.
